name: Hexadecimal
seoDesc: Hexadecimal: a free conversion calculator that walks you through 13 values, with the formula spelled out and a worked example.
summary: The Hexadecimal calculator takes the numbers you enter and reports count immediately. It is free to use, needs no account, and shows the working rather than just the answer. That makes it useful for a recipe, a shopping list, a travel plan or a form that asks for a unit you do not use. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Hexadecimal calculator work?
sections.html:
The Hexadecimal calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports count in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the figures it asks for.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

sections.title: The formula behind the Hexadecimal calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Count=(((((the absolute value of (binary number))) < 22) ? (((the absolute value of (binary number)))) : (((the absolute value of (binary number))) − 5)))
Bits=(4 − ((((((the absolute value of (binary number))) < 22) ? (((the absolute value of (binary number)))) : (((the absolute value of (binary number))) − 5))), 4), 4) + (((((the absolute value of (binary number))) < 22) ? (((the absolute value of (binary number)))) : (((the absolute value of (binary number))) − 5)))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Decimal number = 10, Binary number = 10 and Hexadecimal number = 10. The calculator returns Count = 2 and Bits = 4.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Count = 2 and Bits = 4 should be roughly the size you expected from Decimal number = 10 and Binary number = 10.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Hexadecimal calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a product listing against the measurements you work with
  • Reading a recipe written in units you do not use
  • Converting a figure someone quoted you so you can compare it

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Hexadecimal calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns count. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Hexadecimal calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for a few values, which is 11 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (8 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Count = 2. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Hexadecimal calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
